kid.question: What does Habakkuk tell the earth to do before the Lord in His temple?

options.text: Bow toward Babylon
Bring firstfruits
Keep silent
Light the lamps

kid.explanation: The Lord is in His holy temple, and all the earth is called to keep silence before Him.

kid.question: What does Habakkuk ask the Lord to remember in His wrath?

options.text: Tribute
Mercy
Victory
Sacrifice

kid.explanation: Habakkuk asks the Lord to revive His work and in wrath remember mercy.

kid.question: What do the mountains do when they see the Lord?

options.text: Grow taller
Tremble
Hide the people
Block the rivers

kid.explanation: Habakkuk's prayer pictures the mountains seeing the Lord and trembling before Him.

kid.question: Why does Habakkuk say the Lord went forth in power?

options.text: To crown a new king
To build His temple
To mark new borders
To save His people

kid.explanation: The Lord goes forth for the salvation of His people, with His anointed.

kid.question: What does Habakkuk say he will do even if the crops and herds fail?

options.text: Rejoice in the Lord
Wait in the temple
Fast with the people
Rest beside the fields

kid.explanation: After listing the loss of crops and livestock, Habakkuk says he will still rejoice in the Lord, the God of his salvation.

kid.question: What animal's feet picture the strength God gives Habakkuk?

options.text: A lion's
A horse's
A deer's
A sheep's

kid.explanation: Habakkuk says the Lord is his strength and makes his feet like hinds' feet, enabling him to walk on high places.

kid.question: Who was king when the Lord's word came to Zephaniah?

options.text: Josiah
Hezekiah
Jehoshaphat
Solomon

kid.explanation: Zephaniah's opening dates the word of the Lord to Josiah's reign in Judah.

kid.question: What were some people worshipping on their rooftops?

options.text: The graven calf
The king's image
The sacred grove
The host of heaven

kid.explanation: Zephaniah names those worshipping the host of heaven on housetops among those facing judgment.

kid.question: What will the Lord use to search Jerusalem in Zephaniah's picture?

options.text: Nets
Trumpets
Candles
Scales

kid.explanation: The Lord says He will search Jerusalem with candles and punish those complacent about His action.

kid.question: What sound is named against the fortified cities and towers?

options.text: Shouts of command
Trumpet and alarm
Hoofbeats of horses
Rattling of chariots

kid.explanation: Zephaniah describes the day as one of trumpet and alarm against fenced cities and high towers.

high-school.question: What contrast ends Habakkuk 2?

options.text: A hidden idol stands against the Lord entering the royal palace
A shattered idol stands against the Lord restoring the city walls
A breathless idol stands against the Lord in His holy temple
A treasured idol stands against the Lord withdrawing from His sanctuary

high-school.explanation: Wood and stone are asked to wake despite having no breath; the Lord is in His holy temple and earth is called to silence.

high-school.question: How does Habakkuk hold fear and petition together at the start of his prayer?

options.text: Hearing God frightens him, yet he asks for renewed work and mercy
Hearing God reassures him, so he asks for immediate military command
Hearing God puzzles him, so he asks for another prophet to explain
Hearing God silences him, yet he asks the king to delay the sacrifice

high-school.explanation: Habakkuk says he has heard and feared, then petitions for revival of God's work and mercy within wrath.

high-school.question: What contrast joins the mountains with the Lord's ways?

options.text: The ancient mountains stand and the surrounding nations bow, while His plans change
The new mountains rise and the northern rivers dry, while His promises remain hidden
The new mountains fall and the southern armies flee, while His authority passes to Israel
The ancient mountains scatter and the perpetual hills bow, while His ways endure

high-school.explanation: The everlasting mountains are scattered and perpetual hills bow, but His ways are everlasting.

high-school.question: What goal interprets the frightening images of divine advance?

options.text: The enlargement of His sanctuary
The salvation of His people
The prosperity of His merchants
The appointment of His earthly judges

high-school.explanation: Amid rivers, trembling mountains, weapons, and marching, verse 13 names the salvation of His people as the purpose.

high-school.question: What makes Habakkuk's final rejoicing more than gratitude for a good harvest?

options.text: It follows the arrival of grain from Egypt and cattle from the neighboring peoples
It persists despite failed fruit trees, empty fields, and lost flocks and herds
It celebrates the promised replacement of lost flocks before the coming season of harvest
It follows a royal decree suspending tribute and reopening the markets to foreign merchants

high-school.explanation: The failed fig, vine, olive, field, flock, and herd are followed by joy in God and confidence in His strength.

high-school.question: Which two kinds of failure toward the Lord does Zephaniah condemn together?

options.text: Failure to repair the temple alongside refusal to pay the appointed annual tithe
Neglect of public sacrifices alongside the sale of inherited land to foreign merchants
Refusal of prophetic warnings alongside military alliances with the neighboring royal houses
Worship of rival powers alongside neglect of seeking or inquiring of the Lord

high-school.explanation: The oracle names Baal, heavenly worship, swearing by both the Lord and Malcham, and those who cease seeking or inquiring of Him.

high-school.question: What familiar religious scene is used to announce approaching judgment?

options.text: The Lord prepares a sacrifice and calls the guests He has invited
The Lord appoints new singers and rehearses the procession for the coming festival
The Lord anoints new priests and assigns them places in the sanctuary service
The Lord gathers the firstfruits and distributes them to the families of the Levites

high-school.explanation: The near day of the Lord is framed as His prepared sacrifice with invited guests, followed by punishment of princes and royal children.

high-school.question: Which people are singled out in Zephaniah 1:9, and for what conduct?

options.text: Those entering the sanctuary fill the temple's courts with neglected offerings and vessels
Those guarding the palace fill the king's treasury with withheld wages and stolen tribute
Those leaping on thresholds fill their masters' houses with violence and deceit
Those standing at the gate fill the judges' hands with bribes and false accusations

high-school.explanation: Zephaniah 1:9 pairs those leaping on the threshold with filling their masters' houses through violence and deceit.

high-school.question: What belief is challenged by the searching of Jerusalem?

options.text: The Lord will do neither good nor evil
The Lord will appoint another dynasty in Judah
The Lord will gather the scattered tribes before winter
The Lord will send a second messenger to the royal court

high-school.explanation: Those settled on their lees say God will act neither for good nor for evil; searching and loss answer their complacency.

high-school.question: What connects the unused houses and undrunk vineyard produce?

options.text: People will give their possessions as offerings at the rebuilt temple
People will lose enjoyment of what they have built and planted
People will exchange their property for land across the northern border
People will store their possessions until the next appointed festival

high-school.explanation: Goods become spoil and houses desolate; building and planting do not lead to inhabiting or drinking as the day of trouble approaches.

expert.question: How does the closing contrast of Habakkuk 2 redirect the demand for speech?

options.text: The breathless images are commanded to awaken, then earth is silenced before the Lord
The breathless images are ordered to speak, then priests are summoned to interpret them
The hidden images are ordered to emerge, then kings are summoned to judge their makers
The broken images are ordered to rise, then earth is invited to witness their restoration

expert.explanation: The commands 'Awake' and 'Arise' to lifeless objects are followed by the Lord's presence and earth's commanded silence.

expert.question: What scope is given the Lord's appearance after the naming of Teman and Mount Paran?

options.text: His glory fills the sanctuary and the nations bring tribute to its courts
His glory rests on the mountains and the captives return through the valleys
His glory covers the heavens and the earth is full of His praise
His glory surrounds the capital and the armies gather along its outer walls

expert.explanation: The geographical coming from Teman and Mount Paran opens into a cosmic picture: glory covering the heavens and earth filled with His praise.

expert.question: How are sun and moon placed beside the weapons in Habakkuk's prayer?

options.text: Their rising is set beside the gathering of shields and the march of chariots
Their darkening is set beside the breaking of bows and the burning of enemy armor
Their setting is set beside the fall of swords and the retreat of defeated horsemen
Their standing still is set beside the light of arrows and a glittering spear

expert.explanation: After the trembling mountains and speaking deep, sun and moon stand still in their habitation beside the light of arrows and the shining spear.

expert.question: How does the question about wrath against waters acquire direction in the prayer?

options.text: Chariots of conquest lead toward the replacement of the temple priesthood
Chariots of salvation lead toward the explicit rescue of God's people
Chariots of tribute lead toward the restoration of international commerce
Chariots of exile lead toward the abandonment of God's inherited flock

expert.explanation: The question speaks of chariots of salvation, and verse 13 states that God went forth for His people's salvation.

expert.question: What tension remains between Habakkuk's bodily reaction and his closing confession?

options.text: Trembling coexists with resting, rejoicing, and reliance on God's strength
Trembling ends with withdrawal, silence, and rejection of the earlier vision
Physical confidence coexists with mourning, accusation, and dependence on Assyria
Physical confidence ends with protest, bargaining, and demand for another sign

expert.explanation: Trembling and quivering precede the resolve to rest, rejoice even without provision, and find strength in the Lord.

expert.question: How comprehensive is the imagined material failure before the final 'yet'?

options.text: Fruit trees and vines and flocks in folds fail, but grain and cattle remain
Field crops and herds in stalls fail, but grapes and olives remain for harvest
Field crops and fruit trees fail, but sheep in folds and cattle in stalls remain
Fruit trees and vines, field crops, flocks in folds, and herds in stalls all fail

expert.explanation: The list includes fig, vine, olive, fields, flock, and herd, making the ensuing joy independent of these material supports.

expert.question: What distinction does the rooftop-worship accusation require?

options.text: Some abandon rooftop worship while continuing to neglect their fields
Some replace royal vows with promises to the neighboring tribes
Some swear by the Lord while also swearing by Malcham
Some refuse all worship while still serving in the sanctuary

expert.explanation: The passage targets mixed allegiance as well as Baal worship, heavenly worship, and failure to seek the Lord.

expert.question: How does the sacrifice metaphor affect the command to be silent?

options.text: Silence attends a near judgment pictured as the Lord preparing sacrifice and inviting guests
Silence attends a coming exile pictured as a shepherd driving his flock from pasture
Silence attends a final battle pictured as a farmer gathering his grain for threshing
Silence attends a city siege pictured as a hunter setting his net across the road

expert.explanation: Silence before the Lord accompanies the near day, a prepared sacrifice, invited guests, and specified groups facing punishment.

expert.question: How does the candlelit search develop the judgment on the complacent?

options.text: Their rulers are exiled and their families are divided among the conquerors
Their goods become spoil and their building and planting bring no enjoyment
Their priests are silenced and their festivals are replaced by public mourning
Their fields become saltpits and their houses are occupied by wild creatures

expert.explanation: The candlelit search and threatened spoiling of goods and houses directly confront the claim that God does neither good nor evil.

expert.question: What is the effect of repeating that the great day is near?

options.text: It fixes the approaching judgment after harvest, then describes the starving farmer's bitter cry
It confines the approaching judgment to the coast, then describes the merchant's loss of trade
It makes the approaching judgment urgent, then describes the mighty man's bitter cry
It postpones the approaching judgment until winter, then describes the watchman's final warning

expert.explanation: Nearness and haste precede the mighty man's bitter cry and the catalogue of darkness, desolation, trumpet, and alarm.
